Source: Paul's addendum "Melange Annotated Bibliography — Addendum" (sha12 d09295bf5960), read in full (68 lines). The companion reviewer-annotation file _annots/d09295bf5960.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to add. Entries are Paul's own annotations paraphrased, and citations are recorded as he wrote them; I did not verify them externally.

Overarching argument: the section extends the static influence-maximization entries (Kempe et al. 2003; Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978, covered elsewhere) into a dynamic regime organized in three tiers that mirror the Melange architecture. Tier 1 is one-shot greedy, which is static and submodular and gives the 1-1/e (about 63%) bound. Tier 2 is adaptive greedy, the bridge: a subordinate routine that replans within a campaign as intelligence arrives, with a survival guarantee (Golovin-Krause; CELF makes it computationally practical). Tier 3 is the RL envelope, where a learned outer policy handles cross-campaign compounding, where no greedy guarantee reaches.

Unifying claim: the inner static problem is submodular, the inner sequential problem is adaptive submodular, and the full cross-campaign problem is non-submodular. Paul asserts that RL4CCIM confirms the last point for complex contagion, and that the non-submodular regime is where the durable competitive moat lives.

Systems linked: the operational layer (D* Lite / LPA*, incremental replanning) maps to adaptive submodularity; the strategic layer (MCTS and the orienteering "reach-while-collecting" frame) maps to the RL-IM sequential, long-horizon problem; the political-capital budget maps to GCOMB's budget constraint; the subordinate greedy routine feeds the outer MDP through marginal-influence shaping rewards.

Research questions and implicit hypotheses: (a) whether coalition formation in Congress is a complex contagion (a fence-sitter commits only once enough allies have), which Paul calls "plausibly" true and which would place Melange outside the submodular regime; (b) whether relationship and persuasion costs, unknown a priori, can be learned by probing (Kamarthi); (c) whether lobbying commitment that is probabilistic rather than guaranteed (Chen 2021) changes the seeding policy.

Stated gaps and caveats in the addendum: adaptive submodularity presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard in general, and this is the stated reason Paul still drifts toward learned methods. The frontier paragraph says the four anchored RL entries are "sufficient"; the section in fact anchors seven RL-IM entries plus foundations, so that sentence is loosely worded. The frontier work (MaDGNN) is named without authors or DOI and is not anchored. The Golovin entry's "first to study influence maximization under the adaptive model" is Paul's priority claim and is unverified here.

Overarching argument: Paul asks whether an industry's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal political spending (campaign contributions and lobbying), and whether expected partisan control of Congress shapes the amount and partisan direction of that spending. Five initial sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto (crypto analyzed separately). Hypotheses: H1 deep pockets (positive growth effect); H1-alt distress (negative or asymmetric effect); H2 access-seeking (Republican share rises with expected Republican control); H3 stakes (total contributions rise with a toss-up); H4 lobbying tracks current control more than projected control.

Design synthesis: one distributed-lag model with prior-year and same-year growth (prior-year is the main test, for reverse-causality and timing reasons); pooled panel with sector fixed effects; log CPI-deflated dollars; within-sector z-scored growth; negative-growth indicator; lagged lobbying as a control (cites Kerr, Lincoln & Mishra 2014); projected control as probability of majority (Shift = P minus current majority; Tossup = 1 minus |2P minus 1|), with a directional RShare outcome; year fixed effects as the robustness alternative; wild cluster bootstrap for p-values with 5 clusters and Driscoll-Kraay SEs where year-level terms appear. Cox & Magar (1999) motivates the majority-status (not raw seat) measure.

Stated gaps and self-flagged limits: about 9 elections (2008-2024) so year-level politics variables have little leverage; 5 clusters make inference fragile; same-year growth may be caused by the spending; growth measures not comparable across sectors; OpenSecrets codes do not match NAICS and BEA aggregates banks with credit unions and life insurers with other carriers; regime changes (Citizens United and SpeechNow 2010, McCutcheon 2014, the 2008 LDA quarterly change, the 2024 CUNA-NAFCU merger); crypto donor concentration and Fairshake outside spending; unobserved 501(c) dark money and unregistered lobbying; correlational design only.

Open questions Paul asks (Section 8, 14 numbered): contribution timing (annual vs cycle); what counts as strategic spending; normalization by sector size; probability vs seat change; best historical P measure and odd-year handling; RShare vs alternatives; event study vs regression with about 9 elections; LDA measurement (in-house vs contract, trade associations, shadow lobbying, issue codes); quarterly lobbying; sign of performance-spending relation and anchoring papers (Grier, Munger & Roberts as a starting point); life insurance state regulation (McCarran-Ferguson); sector issue-salience control; estimator choice with lagged DV and few clusters; what reviewers would flag first.

Claims Paul marks for checking (not verified by this read, flag before relying on them): Cox & Magar's about $36,000 per member figure; Cook rating accuracy (about 94% Lean, 97% Likely, 100% Solid); OpenSecrets API discontinued April 15, 2025; Fairshake roughly $260 million over 2023-24; CUNA/NAFCU merger effective January 1, 2024; the six chamber flips (House 2010, 2018, 2022; Senate 2014, 2020, 2024). On the last, the Senate flip usually dated 2020 took effect in January 2021 after the Georgia runoffs, so the year may need a note. Also verify Kerr et al.'s persistence claim and the Cox & Magar corrigendum status.

Other items Paul cites that are not literature works (events and data, not entries): Dodd-Frank (2010), GENIUS Act (2025), McCarran-Ferguson Act, Citizens United, SpeechNow, McCutcheon, LDA reforms, OpenSecrets, DIME, FEC bulk data, LDA.gov API, Iowa Electronic Markets, Cook Political Report, 538 generic ballot, FRED, FDIC, NCUA, ACLI, NAIC, BEA, Fed G.17, CoinGecko/Coin Metrics, IBISWorld.

works.summary:
This is not a research paper. It is the Cook Political Report's House race table from September 12, 2024. For each of the 435 districts it lists the incumbent (or OPEN/VACANT), the Cook PVI and the Cook race rating. It has no method section and no inference. By my substring count of the printed labels there are 25 Toss Ups and 18 Lean races, and the rating totals come to 436 against 435 seats, so the table has a small error. There is also a broken `#REF!` cell at MA-01.

What matters for Paul's system is that **in Cook's own table, PVI and rating do not line up**. The 25 Toss Ups run from R+8 (AK-AL, Peltola) to D+5 (CA-22 Valadao, NY-04 D'Esposito). Seats with the same small lean get very different ratings:
- FL-27 (Salazar) is EVEN and rated Solid R.
- PA-01 (Fitzpatrick) is EVEN and rated Likely R.
- CO-08 and NE-02 are EVEN and rated Toss Up.
- AZ-04 (Stanton) is D+2 and Solid D, while OR-05 (Chavez-DeRemer) is D+2 and Toss Up.

The rating includes incumbent strength and candidate factors that PVI leaves out.

Melange's competitiveness multiplier c (COMPET_MULT, on by default) is a function of Cook PVI alone. With the dial on, it also turns off the receptivity layer's candidate-specific competitiveness term, which came from Ballotpedia vote results. So the system currently treats a safe EVEN-PVI incumbent the same as a true toss-up.

The table is also a dated source of Cook ratings for the sector growth study's `toughness_general` control, which averages Cook, Inside Elections and Sabato ratings on a 0 (safe) to 3 (toss-up) scale, and possibly for the expert-rating path of the seats test. Nothing in the table bears on whether dollars buy more in competitive seats. That reciprocity assumption stays unvalidated. Everything here is my own reading of a single source and is UNVERIFIED until a second check reproduces it (DE-062).

works.title: Should Moving to the Middle Win Candidates Votes? It Depends Where Voters Are
works.summary:
Broockman and Kalla run a pre-registered forced-choice conjoint with 6,000 verified 2024 voters (Verasight, weighted). Respondents choose between hypothetical 2028 presidential pairs of real politicians. On each of three issues, drawn from a bank of 29, each candidate is randomly given either the party's standard position or an "elite middle" position. Pooled, the move to the middle gains Democrats +1.1 pp and Republicans +1.8 pp. The authors argue that this pooled figure hides offsetting effects, so it should only be quoted with its strata. The effect is largest where the party's own position is unpopular (Republicans +3.2 pp in the most liberal-opinion tercile). Where a majority already backs the party's position, the effect is null or negative (Republicans -2.4 pp). At the individual level, voters who hold the party's position punish the move (Republican-position holders -3.6 pp), while voters who disagree reward it. Even "moderate" respondents reward the move only on issues where they disagree with the party, and fewer than 10% answered consistently across five issues. The authors' reading is that voters do vote on issues, but along several dimensions at once, so gains and losses cancel out in the average.

For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on Terrier's canvass layer. Terrier's support score and its "undecided" persuasion term both treat a person's partisan midpoint as the place where persuadability lives. That is a one-dimensional reading. The paper suggests that a mixed partisan score usually marks a cross-pressured voter: someone who can be moved on particular issues and pushed away on others, not a voter persuadable in general. Terrier has no data on voters' issue positions and no input for the candidate's positions, so it cannot represent this. For Melange, the evidence carries over only by analogy, because the paper studies voters, not legislators. Its main structural lesson for Melange is that an average across issues hides offsetting issue-level responses. Any use of this paper in the system stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
works.question: Why do candidates appear to gain only modestly from moving toward the other party's positions, and does that small measured effect mean voters do not vote on issues? The paper asks whether relaxing two common assumptions (that movement toward the other party or the elite middle is movement toward the median voter, and that voter preferences are one-dimensional) can make the measured effect small even when every voter votes on issues.
works.method: Forced-choice conjoint with two candidates (one Democrat, one Republican) per task, each with three randomly assigned issue positions from a bank of 29. Each position is independently assigned to the standard party position or the elite middle position with equal probability. Primary estimand: AMCE of adopting the elite middle position. Estimating equation (Eq. 1, p. 12): Y_ijk = alpha + beta * EliteMiddle_ijk + X_i gamma + e_ijk, estimated separately for Democratic and Republican candidates, with pre-registered pre-treatment covariates (ideology, presidential vote, share liberal in district/state, race, college, party ID 1-7 in Tables A4-A9). Heterogeneity: interactions with policy-domain indicators, terciles of public support for the liberal position (Figure 4), and an indicator for majority support for the party's standard position (Figure 5). Individual-level analyses split by the respondent's own pre-measured issue position (Figures 6-7). Standard errors clustered by respondent; survey weights applied throughout. Pre-registered at OSF (footnote 13). The estimator is described only as a linear model of the form in Eq. 1; the paper does not name it explicitly.

findings.finding: Average effect of adopting the elite middle position (vs standard party position) on one of three issues: Democratic candidates gain 1.1 pp, Republican candidates gain 1.8 pp, both p < 0.001. Described as modest.

Issue heterogeneity is substantial. Democratic effects range from about -1.7 pp (Social Security) to +4.5 pp (affirmative action). Republican effects range from -4.2 pp (transgender sports) to +7.3 pp (gays and lesbians).
findings.numbers: Dem: -1.7 to +4.5 pp; Rep: -4.2 to +7.3 pp

findings.finding: Returns are largest where the party's standard position is least popular. Democrats benefit most on policies where their standard position is furthest from the median voter (more conservative public). Republicans benefit most where the public is liberal. Little benefit where the party already reflects majority sentiment.
findings.numbers: Dem tercile-1 interaction +0.0215 (SE 0.0028), tercile-2 +0.0105 (SE 0.0031), tercile-3 -0.0001 (SE 0.0032); Rep tercile-1 +0.0008 (SE 0.0029), tercile-2 +0.0229 (SE 0.0030), tercile-3 +0.0319 (SE 0.0032). Tercile labels as printed in Table A6.

findings.finding: On issues where a majority prefers the party's standard position, moving to the elite middle has a null or negative effect. The Republican effect is significant (about -2.4 pp, p < 0.001). The Democratic effect is negative and not significant.
findings.numbers: Rep majority-issue -0.0237 (SE 0.0048); Dem majority-issue -0.0042 (SE 0.0041); Rep non-majority +0.0247 (SE 0.0020); Dem non-majority +0.0142 (SE 0.0019)

findings.finding: At the individual level, the same move helps and hurts the same candidate. Respondents who hold the party's standard position on an issue do not reward the elite-middle move and may penalize it. Republican candidates lose among respondents who hold the Republican position (about -3.6 pp). Democratic respondents with the Democratic position show a non-significant effect.

Respondents classified as overall moderate (mixed positions across issues) still reward moving to the elite middle only on issues where they disagree with the party's standard position. Moderates who agree with the Republican position on an issue penalize Republican candidates who move to the elite middle.
findings.location: pp. 20-21; Figure 7; Table A9 (Table A9 covers the moderate subsample)
findings.numbers: Rep candidate, own=R -0.0524 (SE 0.0112); Rep candidate, own=D +0.0381 (SE 0.0072); Dem candidate, own=D -0.0011 (SE 0.0113), own=R +0.0239 (SE 0.0069). Per Table A9's note, the moderate subsample is N(Dem) = 5,056-7,983 and N(Rep) = 4,806-10,404 across columns.

related.why: It quantifies returns to political microtargeting by subgroup, the operational counterpart to this paper's finding that persuasion response differs by issue and by voter position.
It tests microtargeted persuasion with generative AI. This paper explains why tailoring by issue should matter: cross-pressured voters respond with opposite signs on different issues.

D-NOMINATE gives the low-dimensional account of elite roll-call ideology. This paper argues mass opinion is multidimensional relative to the elite axis, which is why elite-middle moves do not map onto a single median voter.
CFscores place donors and candidates on one ideological dimension. This paper's cross-pressure finding cautions against reading a single-axis position as a position on any particular issue.
An agent-based model of micro-targeted campaigning. Issue-specific, voter-position-dependent responses of the kind measured here are the empirical input such a model would need.

works.title: Which Narrative Strategies Durably Reduce Prejudice? Evidence from Field and Survey Experiments Supporting the Efficacy of Perspective-Getting
works.summary:
Kalla and Broockman (AJPS 2023, vol. 67, pp. 185-204; DOI 10.1111/ajps.12657, so the vault slug's 2020 year and OSF DOI are wrong) take apart the deep-canvass conversation. They test which narrative step actually reduces exclusionary attitudes toward unauthorized immigrants and transgender people. Study 1 (MI, PA, NC, fall 2019; about 2,975 voters per arm) found that dropping analogic perspective-taking did not weaken effects, which lasted at least 4.5 months. Dichotomized health-policy items moved 5 to 9 points. In Study 2 (CA and TN, 2020; about 2,050 per arm, stopped early by COVID), a perspective-getting-only script took 7.3 minutes against 17.1 for the full script. It matched the full script: the 95% CI on the difference ran from -0.05 to 0.09 SD. Scholarship support rose 12.7 points and in-state-tuition support 7.4. A non-randomized phone follow-up gave about 0.12 SD. The within-subject analyses and a nine-arm meta-regression point the same way, but both are observational. Effects are intent-to-treat among people who came to the door, about 81 to 82% of whom engaged. All outcomes are explicit issue attitudes; votes and turnout were not measured.

For Paul's systems the paper bears only on Terrier's canvass layer, and only loosely. Untapped potential picks *whom* to knock on a prior that persuasion peaks at 50% candidate support. The paper says nothing about that prior. What it shows is that the effect depends on *what is said* at the door, and that a script half as long can work just as well. Nothing in Melange's legislator-facing engine is touched, because these are voter attitude experiments, not studies of elites, lobbying or networks. The paper also is not the 'Kalla & Broockman' that the flip model's money-buys-access comment cites.
works.question: Which narrative strategies used in interpersonal conversation (analogic perspective-taking, vicarious perspective-giving, perspective-getting; and traditional perspective-taking in a survey) durably reduce exclusionary attitudes toward unauthorized immigrants and transgender people, and through which mechanisms?
works.method: Field RCTs with placebo arms, pre-registered outcome indices (first factor of a factor analysis of the pre-registered items, standardized). Study 1 and 2: OLS with pre-treatment covariates, standard errors clustered by household, intent-to-treat among those who identified themselves at the door. Within-subject (not pre-registered in Study 1): difference-in-differences with survey-wave and individual fixed effects, indicator for post-treatment wave interacted with whether the canvasser or voter shared each narrative type, SEs clustered by individual, treatment arms only. Study 3: difference-in-differences comparing change among reached and unreached people, without an uncontacted control group (Table 2 note, p.188), so the estimate is close to a complier-average effect. Pooled within-subject estimate is precision-weighted across Studies 1-3 (Fig 6). Meta-regression: random-effects, study-level clustering, dummies for presence of each narrative in each arm (p.197 to p.198). Survey experiment: linear regression with pre-registered pretreatment covariates, Identified Photo arm as baseline, separate scales for each outgroup, and a mediator battery (Fig 8).

findings.finding: Abstract summary: conversations employing only perspective-getting narratives durably reduce exclusionary attitudes; omitting analogic perspective-taking and vicarious perspective-giving does not diminish effects; perspective-getting consistently reduces exclusionary attitudes across all designs.
findings.numbers: No numeric effect sizes in the abstract.

findings.finding: Study 1: removing the analogic perspective-taking step did not reduce effects. The full intervention and the version without analogic perspective-taking were similarly effective, and the latter was slightly larger; effects persisted for at least 4.5 months.
findings.numbers: Baseline randomized n = 2,973 (Full), 2,975 (without analogic), 2,977 (Placebo); 369,317 mailed; effect sizes only in Fig 1 (not in extracted text).

findings.finding: Study 1 dichotomized health-policy items: both treatments moved respondents into support, and the without-analogic version was always similar to or larger than the full version.
findings.numbers: Increases of 5 to 9 percentage points on dichotomized health-care policy items.

findings.finding: Study 1 within-subject (observational, not pre-registered): voters who heard a story about an immigrant (perspective-getting) had significantly higher overall index changes; voters who told a story about someone they know (vicarious) showed a negative, insignificant change; analogic stories had no significant added change.
findings.numbers: Point estimates in Fig 3 only; vicarious estimate negative and insignificant; perspective-getting significant (values not in text).

findings.finding: Study 2 (randomized): perspective-getting-only conversations had effects similar to the full intervention, and both were statistically significant on the overall index. The full-minus-perspective-getting-only comparison was nearly zero, and the authors judge the difference to be noise that warrants replication.
findings.numbers: Overall-index 95% CI on Full minus PG-only from 0.09 to -0.05 SD; Full n = 2,053, PG-only n = 2,054, Placebo n = 2,056.

findings.finding: Study 2 durability and duration: effects persisted at least 11 weeks; at 4.5 months the Full arm had p = .07 and the PG-only arm p = .24 (not significant). Perspective-getting-only conversations took about half the time.
findings.location: p.196 to p.197 (footnote to 4.5-month p-values); p.195 (timing)
findings.numbers: Full conversation averaged 17.1 minutes; PG-only averaged 7.3 minutes.

related.why: Same authors. It addresses where voters sit and when candidate moderation pays, which bears on Terrier's candidate-support s and the s=0.5 persuasion peak. This paper instead addresses which door conversation durably moves attitudes.

Same authors, different study. It is the money-buys-access field experiment that flip_model.py:21 actually cites. Keeping the two distinct prevents misattributing persuasion evidence to the flip model.

It quantifies the persuasive returns to targeting messages by audience. This paper shows message content (perspective-getting) carries the effect. Together they separate who-to-target from what-to-say, the split Terrier's potential formula collapses into target selection.
A microtargeting persuasion study. It is a contrast to interpersonal narrative persuasion when deciding whether Terrier's persuade term should model the message or only the target.

works.title: Old money: Campaign finance and gerontocracy in the United States
works.summary:
Bonica and Grumbach link DIME itemized FEC contributions to the L2 voter file and to candidate birth years. They show that US federal campaign money is much older than the electorate. In the 2020 cycle, the median contribution dollar comes from a 66-year-old, the median donor is 59, and only 9% of dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger. For comparison, the median general-election voter is 52, the median primary voter is 59 and the median non-voter is 39. Within districts, each year of candidate age adds about 0.21 years to average donor age (N = 6,098 candidate-cycles, 2012-2020). Within donors, using two-way fixed effects on 2020 donor-candidate pairs, a larger age gap lowers the chance of giving. The authors put a 30-year gap at about a 50% lower donating rate. The coefficient is -0.00328 for Democrats and -0.00317 for Republicans on a x100 scale. Pre-2020 Republican estimates are unstable because of WinRed coverage. Seed money, defined as the first 50 donations, is older and larger for older non-incumbent House candidates (N = 931). A voucher reweighting, which is a counterfactual and not an estimate, would raise funds for candidates under 66. The paper is descriptive and states that it identifies no causal effect of wealth or of policy.

For Paul's systems, its main use is as a measurement warning, not as an engine parameter. Terrier's Sphere and Participation standings run on vendor fields for political giving and turnout. The paper shows both are steeply age-graded. Terrier stratifies standings by registration but not by age, so its top deciles will lean older. Mentat's identity ladder and conduit handling line up with the paper's own data hazards: linkage built to avoid false positives, and small-donor itemization that is only complete from 2020. The paper does not bear on the Moneyball ranking, the cascade engine or the SNA layers.
works.question: How unequal is money in US politics across generations, and does this inequality affect political representation? (a) Age distribution of donors, voters, candidates and officeholders; (b) whether donors give more often and more per gift to candidates closer to their age; (c) whether seed (early) fundraising depends on candidate age; (d) how a voucher policy would change candidate fundraising by age.
works.method: Descriptive: age distributions for 2020 (box plots, medians and dollar-weighted means), generational shares of wealth vs donations (Fig. 6), and birth-cohort representational weight = cohort share of contributions over population share, scaled to 18-year-olds = 1 (Fig. 4). Candidate-level OLS (Eq. 1): average donor age (or dollar-weighted average) on candidate age x incumbency, with cycle and district fixed effects (Table 1). Donor-level linear probability model (Donated x100) and asinh(amount) (Eq. 2): |Age Gap| between donor and candidate, same-state control, donor and candidate two-way fixed effects, separately for Democrats and Republicans, with generation interactions (Tables 2-3; text p. 8-9). Seed-funding OLS with district fixed effects (Table 4). Counterfactual voucher simulation (Sec. 6.1, pp. 12-13): post-stratification reweighting of contributions so that strata (birth year, precinct partisanship in 10 groups, population density in 5 bins) match electoral shares, via inflation factor eta_s = electoral share / contribution share; gamma_c = voucher-program contributions / actual contributions per candidate; log(gamma_c) plotted by candidate age with loess (Fig. 8).

findings.finding: Median dollar of campaign contributions comes from a 66-year-old; mean dollar from a 64-year-old (63.9); median unweighted donor is 59. Only 9% of contribution dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger.
findings.numbers: median dollar 66; mean dollar 63.9; median donor 59; 9% of dollars from donors <=40

findings.finding: Age gaps in participation: median voter 52, median non-voter 39, median primary voter 59. Average American age 38; voting-age public age 47. Candidates slightly younger than donors; incumbents slightly older. Those gaps are smaller than the gap between donors and general-election voters or non-voters.
findings.numbers: voters 52; non-voters 39; primary voters 59; donors 59; US average 38; voting-age public 47

findings.finding: Generational shares of donations track wealth shares. Baby Boomers give 53.6% of donation dollars and receive 48.5% of candidate receipts; Millennials give 5% of donation dollars and receive 10.4% of candidate receipts. Millennial candidates get over 66% of their dollars from Silent and Boomer donors plus about 20% from Gen X; Millennial donors supply 4% of Boomer candidates' receipts.
findings.location: Sec. 5.1 p. 7 (Fig. 6); Sec. 4.1 p. 6 and Appendix A7 for wealth shares
findings.numbers: Boomer donors 53.6%; Millennial donors 5%; Millennial candidate receipts 10.4%; Millennial candidates 66%+ from Silent/Boomers; Gen X ~20%; Millennial share of Boomer-candidate money 4%; wealth shares Millennials 4.5%, Boomers 53.1%; contributions Millennials 5.3%, Boomers 52.8%

findings.finding: Representational weight rises sharply with age. 35-year-olds are over 25 times better represented than 18-year-olds; the most represented cohorts (ages 70-80) give about 200-300 times more per capita than the youngest cohort.
findings.numbers: 35-year-olds >25x 18-year-olds; ages 70-80 200-300x youngest cohort per capita

findings.finding: Average contribution size rises with donor birth cohort. Donors born after 1985 give about $75 on average; donors born 1940-1965 about $200; pre-1935 cohorts about $300. Ever-donors to the $2,900 limit average 63 years old.
findings.location: Sec. 5.1 / Fig. 5 p. 6 and Sec. 6 p. 11
findings.numbers: post-1985 ~$75; 1940-1965 ~$200; pre-1935 ~$300; limit-donors average age 63

findings.finding: Candidate age is strongly associated with donor age within districts. Each year of candidate age raises average donor age by about 0.21 years (unweighted) and dollar-weighted donor age by about 0.20 years. Donor-age SD is 5.8 vs 12.5 for candidate age. Incumbents have donors about 8 years older on average (unweighted).
findings.numbers: 0.21 (SE 0.01); 0.20 (SE 0.01); N = 6,098 candidate-cycles; incumbent +8.16 years; SD donor age 5.8, candidate age 12.5

related.why: Both rest on DIME contribution records and CFscores. This paper uses DIME v4.0 and cites the database but not this paper by name.
Cited at p. 3 as field-experiment evidence that donors get meetings with legislators more often than non-donor constituents. The paper relies on it for its link from donating to access.
The donor-level models are two-way fixed-effects regressions. Imai and Kim's cautions about reading 2FE as causal apply. Not cited.
Both have to resolve individual identities in FEC data. Kim et al. use constrained graph clustering, and Bonica and Grumbach use precision-first name and address linkage to L2. Not cited.
Bonica and Grumbach study individual contributions only and exclude PACs. Furnas et al. separate PAC money from lobbying money, which shows which money stream each claim covers. Not cited.

works.title: Mapping the Ideological Marketplace
works.summary:
Bonica (SSRN draft, 2013) estimates common-space ideal points (CFscores) for candidates and donors. The data are more than 100 million federal and state contribution records from 1979 to 2012, and the method is correspondence analysis on a contributor-by-recipient matrix. Donors who give in both state and federal races bridge the two levels. Pooled across parties, candidate CFscores track DW-NOMINATE at r = 0.92 (unstratified). Within party the correlation is much weaker: 0.56 to 0.72. Scores for non-incumbents predict their later roll-call scores about as well as incumbent scores do.

For this system, the important result is the test of why people give. On 5,000 individual donors with 25 or more federal gifts (2004-2012), the ideological model beats both the partisan electoral model and the investor model by log-likelihood. The investor model barely beats the baseline. For corporate and trade PACs the investor model is competitive, and in its unconstrained form it fits better than the ideological model (Table 2). That is why those PACs are left out of estimation.

Three consequences follow:
1. The paper does not show that dollars buy more in competitive seats. The partisan electoral model, which Paul highlighted, loses to the ideological model for individual donors.
2. CU and bank PAC money is exactly the mixed-motive class. Because individual donors give by ideology, money and stance are entangled, so any test of whether money moves members needs an ideology control.
3. The record-linkage appendix gives Mentat's identity ladder a concrete error profile. When merges went wrong, they joined family members at the same employer.

The paper measures who gives and why. It does not test whether giving changes votes or buys access, so it cannot calibrate any money-response constant.
works.question: How can ideal points be estimated for candidates and contributors across federal and state elections, for incumbents and non-incumbents, from campaign contribution records? Secondary: whether ideology or strategic motives (investor, partisan-electoral) drive contributions, and whether the resulting common-space CFscores are valid and stable enough for work on polarization, state politics, candidate positioning and donor ideology.
works.method: Augmented correspondence analysis (CA) on the contributor-by-recipient contingency matrix R (PDF p.7; supplement). Matrix is standardized and decomposed by SVD of K = D_r^(-1/2)(R - rc')D_c^(-1/2); contributor ideal points theta = U D^-1/2 scaled, recipient delta = V D^-1/2. CA is described as nearly equivalent to a log-linear ideal point model (Lowe 2008; ter Braak 1985). Steps: (1) scale federal elections first; (2) scale each state separately, using bridge contributors (those giving to both state and federal races), with an 8-step alternating least-squares routine; (3) jointly re-estimate recipients; (4) normalize so the weighted mean and SD of contribution amounts are 0 and 1. Between-set identification: contributor points are regressed on matched candidate points with an error-in-variables specification (intercept 0.017, slope 0.975, on 29,913 candidates who appear as donors). Presidential nominees get separate pre- and post-nomination scores. Non-incumbent scores: contributor points held fixed; candidate points re-estimated from pre-record contributions. Period-specific CFscores follow Nokken and Poole (2004). Strategic-giving comparison: a right-censored negative binomial count model per donor (IRT-style, adapted from Bonica 2013a), compared by log-likelihood and the Cameron-Windmeijer deviance residual RDev.

findings.finding: Candidate CFscores correlate with common-space DW-NOMINATE at r = 0.92. Within-party correlations are weaker: House Democrats 0.56, House Republicans 0.66, Senate Democrats 0.64, Senate Republicans 0.72. Figure 1 totals: House incumbents 0.91, open seats 0.93, challengers 0.89; Senate incumbents 0.91, open seats 0.95, challengers 0.92.
findings.location: External Validity, PDF p.11 (Fig. 1 on PDF p.13)
findings.numbers: r=0.92; within-party House D 0.56 / R 0.66; Senate D 0.64 / R 0.72

findings.finding: Non-incumbent CFscores predict future DW-NOMINATE about as well as incumbent CFscores. Incumbent and non-incumbent CFscores correlate highly, and within-party correlations are lower for Democrats.
findings.numbers: non-incumbent vs incumbent CFscore r = 0.96 overall, 0.93 R, 0.88 D

findings.finding: Roll-call classification: CFscores classify votes nearly as well as roll-call measures, although they never condition on roll calls. Party-only classification is also reported.
findings.numbers: House (96th-112th): CFscore 0.880 (APRE 0.638), DW-NOMINATE 0.896 (0.687), Turbo-ADA 0.886 (0.659), party 0.863 (0.588). Senate: CFscore 0.870 (0.607), DW-NOMINATE 0.882 (0.644), party 0.838 (0.514)

findings.finding: Period-specific stability: CFscores are more stable across periods than DW-NOMINATE. The text states the result as greater inter-temporal stability.
findings.numbers: R2 of static on period-specific: CFscore 0.97 overall, 0.89 D, 0.86 R; DW-NOMINATE House 0.96 (0.86 D, 0.70 R), Senate 0.96 (0.72 D, 0.85 R)

findings.finding: Donor-candidate consistency: candidates who also donate have CFscores as contributors that track their CFscores as recipients. The author reads this as both activities expressing the same latent ideology.
findings.numbers: r = 0.94 overall, 0.78 D, 0.68 R among 10,406 candidates who gave to at least 5 recipients (of 29,913 candidates who made contributions)

findings.finding: Individual donors give on ideology: the ideological model beats both strategic models for individuals. The investor model barely improves on the baseline. Investor model fits better than the ideological model for about 5% of individual donors. For corporate and trade PACs the investor model is competitive with the ideological model, which supports excluding those PACs from estimation.
findings.numbers: Log-lik individuals: unrestricted -1,275,233; ideological -1,334,200; partisan -1,405,855; investor -1,504,601; unconstrained investor -1,468,435; baseline -1,520,312. Labor PACs: ideological -231,022; investor -252,936. Corp/trade PACs: ideological -1,694,458; investor -1,695,149; unconstrained investor -1,687,949. RDev for individuals: ideological 0.601, investor 0.412.

related.why: Same campaign-finance contributor data family. The 2013 text does not cite the 2025 work, so builds-on runs the wrong direction; the later work builds on this data.
The paper uses Poole and Rosenthal common-space DW-NOMINATE as the roll-call benchmark (r = 0.92 pooled, text PDF p.10). Table 1 is classification rates, not that correlation.
Not cited in this paper. Conceptual pairing only: the investor model tests access-type motives without measuring access. Kalla's content is not verified against this text.

works.title: Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials: A Randomized Field Experiment
works.summary:
Kalla and Broockman ran a blocked randomized field experiment in 2013. CREDO Action asked 191 House offices for a district meeting about a chemical-ban bill. All offices belonged to one party and none had cosponsored the bill. In one office per covariate-matched triplet (64 offices, a number derived from the design), the request called the attendees "local campaign donors". The other 127 offices were told "local constituents", and nothing else changed. The outcome was the rank of the most senior official who attended. Over June to August 2013, a chief of staff or more senior official attended in 12.5% of donor-label offices and 2.4% of constituent-label offices (p=.006). For legislative director or above the figures were 18.8% and 5.5% (p=.005), and for the Member personally 7.8% and 2.4% (p=.07). Lower-ranked staff showed no reliable difference (48.4% vs 43.3% at any district staffer or above, p=.26). The ordered probit gave p=.05.

The randomized treatment was the donor label, not real money. The paper cannot say why the label works, and it measures access, not influence. Only 9 offices cosponsored during the study, so the cosponsorship comparison tells us nothing.

For Paul's systems, the paper mainly bounds an existing citation. flip_model.py:21 cites Kalla and Broockman for "money buys access/effort > votes" and labels the 0.35/0.65 money/peer split CALIBRATED. The paper supports the access half of that line. It says nothing about votes, positions, cosponsorship or the money-to-peer ratio, so it cannot calibrate those constants.

The paper's best transferable idea is its outcome measure: the seniority of the official who takes the meeting. The prospective contract and the staffer routes have no outcome of that kind. The contract scores new cosponsorships, which is the same low-base-rate outcome that left this paper uninformative. Nothing here supports the competitiveness multiplier.
works.question: Can an interest group obtain superior access to senior congressional officials because its members have donated to political campaigns? Put as a counterfactual: would House offices have treated the same group members differently had the offices not known they were donors? (p.545, p.548)
works.method: Blocked randomized field experiment. Offices were blocked into 64 triplets using blockTools (Mahalanobis distance) on six covariates; one office per block randomly assigned to Revealed Donor and two to Constituent (pp.549-550). The request e-mail described attendees as "local campaign donors" (Revealed Donor) or "local constituents" (Constituent); nothing else varied, and correspondence was standardized by a prespecified protocol (pp.550-551). Outcome: the rank of the official who would attend, recorded more than 24 hours in advance and confirmed after the meeting, coded into six ordered categories by two coders blind to assignment (p.552). Analysis: exact p-values from randomization inference under the sharp null, one comparison per cumulative rank; Bonferroni check across five comparisons; ordered probit with randomization-inference p-value as an omnibus test (pp.552-554).

findings.finding: Senior access rose when the donor label was revealed: chief of staff or above was available in 12.5% of Revealed Donor offices vs 2.4% of Constituent offices (cumulative), p=.006 by randomization inference.
Legislative director or deputy chief of staff or above: 18.8% vs 5.5% (cumulative), p=.005. The text describes this as more than a threefold increase.
Member of Congress meetings: 7.8% vs 2.4%, p=.07. Not significant at .05 on its own, though the text describes it as more than three times as likely.

Abstract summary: senior policy makers were available between three and four times more often when the donor label was revealed. Ratios implied by Table 1 are about 3.2x (Member), 3.4x (LD or above), 5.2x (chief of staff or above).
findings.numbers: 3-4x (abstract); 3.2x, 3.4x, 5.2x (derived)

findings.finding: Lower-ranked staff showed no reliable difference: DC-based legislative assistant or local district director cumulative 37.5% vs 30.7%, p=.17; other district-based staffer cumulative 48.4% vs 43.3%, p=.26.

Any meeting: the text says 56.7% of Constituent and 51.6% of Revealed Donor offices scheduled any meeting, and that about half of offices granted meetings overall. Table 1 instead labels 56.7% and 51.6% as 'No Meeting', which reverses the text's meaning. The table columns sum to 100% under the 'No Meeting' reading, so the text wording looks inconsistent with the table.
findings.location: Text p.552 and p.553 (lines on 'scheduled any meeting'); Table 1 p.552
findings.numbers: 56.7% vs 51.6% (label conflict)

related.why: Survey experiment on 441 DC congressional staffers about money and information. Together with this field experiment it bears on the mechanism question the authors leave open.
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters test whether donations precede lobbying on bills in observational LDA and FEC data. This randomized donor label supports the access step those sequences assume.
Furnas, LaPira and Brock show low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which limits how often a donor label is available to lobbying actors.
Blackwell and Yamauchi address unmeasured confounding in observational political-ad effects after Citizens United, the confounding problem this randomized design avoids.

Bonica and Grumbach show campaign money is much older than the electorate and wealth is concentrated. Their text also cites this paper's donor-access result. Relevant to who can credibly present as a donor.
Holyoke, Brown and LaPira describe lobbyist relationships built on mutual need. This experiment shows the donor signal shifts which staff tier engages.

works.title: How Dark Is It? An Investigation of Dark Money Operations in U.S. Nonprofit Political Advocacy Organizations
works.summary:
Irvin builds a nine-part opacity index from IRS Form 990 fields, plus one website word count, and applies it to 54 501(c)(4) economic-policy advocacy groups using 2016 filings (25 right-leaning, 2 centrist, 27 left-leaning). The components are board size, volunteers, website length, related 527s, related 501(c)(3)s, the share of spending that is political or lobbying, the salary share, the size of reserves and fundraising intensity. Each is scaled 0-1 and the nine are summed with equal weight, so the index runs 0-9. Scores ranged from 0.8 to 8.3. The most opaque groups had one or two board members, almost no staff, very short websites and large grants to affiliated PACs. For example, One Nation spent $63.3M in 2016 and granted $21.7M to the Senate Leadership Fund. Validation is weak. Thirteen of the 54 groups appear on OpenSecrets' 2016 dark-money list, and that label correlates with four of the nine components. But in a logistic regression with controls, the total index does not predict the label (Nagelkerke R2 0.529; only log expenses is significant). The paper also describes this political spending as mostly negative, based on Beckel 2018, without a count.

For Paul's systems this matters mainly in Mentat. The transfer graph traces only FEC committee-to-committee transfers (24G/24K). Money a 501(c)(4) gives a Super PAC therefore enters as a receipt with no upstream path. Separately, under Paul's 2026-07-18 ruling, 501c recipients are excluded from reported totals. The paper shows that excluded group mixes transparent policy shops with near-shell political vehicles. It does not show that the index can tell them apart reliably. Nothing in the paper bears on Melange's member ranking, stance, SNA or Terrier.

works.title: Understanding Partisan Cue Receptivity: Tests of Predictions from the Bounded Rationality and Expressive Utility Perspectives
works.summary:
Bakker, Lelkes and Malka ran four US survey experiments, plus two ancillary ones and a pooled individual-data meta-analysis, on partisans in online panels from 2016 to 2018. The issues (food irradiation and farm subsidies) were chosen because they were not yet partisan. The paper tests two accounts of why people follow party cues. Bounded rationality says low-resource citizens use cues to save effort. Expressive utility says strong identifiers with high cognitive resources use cues to protect their party identity.

Bounded rationality gets no support. Cue effects are no larger among low-CRT, low-NfC or low-knowledge respondents, and most interaction signs run the other way. Expressive utility gets partial support. In the meta-analysis, among high-resource respondents the in-party cue effect rises with partisan identity strength (slope .15 for NfC and latent resources), about 15 points from the weakest to the strongest identifiers. Only two of six three-way terms are significant, and the MTurk replication shows nothing.

The finding that matters most for Melange is the main-effect asymmetry. The out-party cue reduces support by .06 to .07 on a 0-1 scale, which is a significant repulsion. The in-party cue adds only about +.03 and is non-significant in studies 1 and 2. The engine cites this paper (paired with Furnas) for `cpf_pressure`, which scores co-partisan pressure at x1.7 and out-partisan pressure at a positive x0.5. The paper shows something different: out-party cues push the receiver away, and in-party cues are weak.

The subjects are members of the public reading one-shot survey vignettes, not legislators pressing other legislators. The evidence is therefore a direction-of-sign check for the engine, not a source for its constants.
works.question: Why do citizens follow partisan cues when forming policy judgments? Is cue receptivity strongest among people with low cognitive resources (bounded rationality, cue-taking as effort-saving), or among people with both strong partisan social identity and high cognitive resources (expressive utility, effortful identity-protective reasoning)?
works.method: OLS regression of policy support on in-party and out-party cue dummies (control is omitted category), partisan social identity strength (PSID), one cognitive resource measure, and covariates (gender, age, education, race, party). The bounded rationality test uses cue-by-resource and cue-by-PSID two-way interactions. The expressive utility test uses cue x PSID x resource three-way interactions, plotted as marginal effects at -1 SD, mean, and +1 SD of PSID and resources. Individual-data meta-analysis (studies 1-4, and separately seven experiments for the in-party vs out-party contrast) uses mixed-effects regression with dummies for studies and random intercepts for study and individual. Studies 3 and 4 also measured depth of processing (reading time, thought-listing word count, factual quiz) to test the proposed mechanism.

findings.finding: No support for the bounded rationality prediction. Cue effects are not stronger among low cognitive resource respondents, and in several cases the interaction points the opposite way.
findings.location: Abstract p. 1061; study 1 p. 1065; study 2 p. 1066; meta-analysis p. 1070
findings.numbers: Study 1: none of six cue x resource interactions significant; in 5 of 6 the sign is opposite to the BR prediction. Study 2: all eight cue x resource interactions opposite to BR; seven nonsignificant, one significant (political knowledge x out-party cue).

findings.finding: Study 1 main effects: out-party cue reduces support; in-party cue effect not significant.
findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.06 points on 0-1 scale (p < .01); in-party cue +0.03 (not significant). N = 747.

findings.finding: Study 1, expressive utility (NfC): among high need-for-cognition respondents, the in-party cue effect grows with partisan identity strength; the three-way term is significant for in-party cue only. CRT and latent-resource three-way terms are not significant.
findings.location: Study 1, p. 1065-1066; Table 2 model 4; Figure 1 middle row
findings.numbers: In-party x NfC x PSID b = 1.08 (SE .49, p = .027). Simple slope of in-party cue on PSID among high NfC b = .26 (SE .11, p = .019). Out-party analogue b = -.14 (SE .11), not significant. Out-party three-way b = -.53 (SE .51).

findings.finding: Study 2, expressive utility: out-party cue effect is larger for strongly identified partisans among high-CRT respondents; political knowledge gives a similar out-party pattern; NfC and latent-resource terms point the expected way but are not significant.
findings.numbers: CRT: out-party x PSID x CRT b = -.78 (SE .34, p = .02); in-party three-way b = .29 (SE .37), not significant. Among high-CRT respondents, strong identifiers were more influenced by out-party cues than weak identifiers, b = -.27 (SE .12, p = .02); no parallel for in-party cue. Political knowledge: out-party three-way b = -.68 (SE .28, p = .02); in-party b = .54 (SE .28, p = .05, nearly significant).

findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.07 on 0-1 scale; in-party cue no significant influence. N = 1,302 in text (Table 3 note reports N = 1,258).

findings.finding: Replications (study 3, Bovitz Forthright, and study 4, MTurk) do not support the expressive utility or bounded rationality model in the same way as studies 1 and 2. Study 3 shows again no BR support and mixed EU support; study 4 shows no support for either model.
findings.location: Pp. 1069; appendices C.1-C.2 (study 3) and D.1-D.5 (study 4); discussion pp. 1073-1074; fn. 18 p. 1076
findings.numbers: Study 3 N = 1,911; study 4 N = 2,509 (Table 1). Study 4 showed no trace of the patterns in other studies; its CRT means were significantly higher than study 3 (app. D.5).

Observational counterpart on elite party cues and out-party backlash. Item file exists; its content was not re-checked here.

works.title: Cross-Industry Political Spending - Analysis Overview (memo)
works.summary:
An unsigned internal memo dated 12/10/2025. Names are redacted and it is not peer-reviewed. It profiles federal political giving by the top 10 firms by revenue in four industries: life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions and commercial banking. It splits that giving across CEOs, other executives, company PACs, trade associations (ACLI, ACU, ABA) and the four largest Super PACs. Its headline claim is that firms push political spending onto executives and adjust their giving to executive-branch scrutiny "regardless of party". The evidence is per-industry dollar averages, which carry no cycle years, source or N, plus news-driven case stories: Bank of America after the DOJ probe, JPMorgan's PAC memos, and the Schwab charity fund. There is no comparison group and no test. The memo reports its own ranking contradictions, and it uses "dark money" to mean Super PAC money.

For Paul's systems the memo is a descriptive input, not evidence. Its unit of analysis is the same one Mentat's spending-statistics sheet already builds. That sheet has role tiers (Chief, Middle Management, Employee, Corporate) and channel columns (Super PAC, Company PAC, Trade Association, Candidate, Company PAC to Super PAC, each with a partisan split). Mentat also ingests a "Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx" template. The memo may therefore come from the same product line, and if it does it is not an independent check. Two parts are useful. First, the bank, mutual-fund and CU stories show giving moving into channels that per-member models never see: trade associations, Super PACs, and family or charity vehicles. That bears on how Melange's flip model measures competitor money. Second, its partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore whether the money supported or opposed a candidate, which Mentat already separates. Every figure in the memo should be treated as UNVERIFIED, with no window or denominator.
works.question: Whether executive and corporate political spending in four industries (life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions, commercial banking; top 10 by revenue each) is offloaded onto company executives, and whether these industries adapt their giving to executive-branch pressure and scrutiny "regardless of party" (Overview, line 11).
works.method: Descriptive only. Per-industry averages of CEO and executive spending in dollars. Trade association average donations and cumulative industry PAC totals. Ratios of outside giving to PAC giving (life insurance, line 16). Share of Super PAC money originating from the company rather than individuals (JPMorgan, +90%, line 21). Qualitative characterization of year-to-year volatility (line 25) and partisan split (lines 24, 40-42). Qualitative review of internal memos, employee communications, interviews, and news reports of DOJ and executive-order actions.

Life insurance: CEO average spending and executive average spending across the top 10 firms. Ranked 3rd of four industries in raw spending.

findings.numbers: ACLI CEO avg $3,000; executive avg $1,166; ACLI PAC avg $911,470

findings.numbers: CEO outside:PAC 1.15:1; executive PAC:outside 1.54:1 (memo's wording)

Furnas, LaPira and Brock find low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending. That supports the memo's premise that money moves across channels and warns against treating one channel as total effort.

works.title: Party Cues in the News: Democratic Elites, Republican Backlash and the Dynamics of Climate Skepticism
works.summary:
Merkley and Stecula ask whether climate skepticism in the US public grew because people reacted against Democratic elites, with news coverage carrying those cues. They combine three methods. First, a Lexicoder dictionary flags party cues in NYT and WaPo climate coverage. Second, they run time-series models on a latent skepticism index built from about 172 poll questions. Third, they run a 2019 MTurk experiment with N=2,970.

In the time series, the share of articles carrying Democratic cues Granger-causes skepticism, both in the aggregate (chi2 6.96, p=0.01) and among Republicans (chi2 7.35, p=0.03). The reverse direction does not hold. Republican cues have no aggregate effect (p=0.94). In the experiment, a single Democratic cue moves strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism on a 0-1 scale (about 0.2 SD). A polarized cue, Democrats for and Republicans against, moves them +0.09. A consensus cue, with Republicans joining Democrats, produces no movement and does not depolarize. More coverage alone, with cues held fixed, goes with lower Republican skepticism (-0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter). The Granger tests show only which series moves first, not causation. The causal evidence is one MTurk experiment on mass partisans, not legislators.

For Melange, the paper's value is about direction. An out-party cue is not a weaker positive cue. Among mass partisans it pushes the other way. Three parts of the engine encode out-party cues differently:
- The cascade kernel's cpf_pressure gives an out-party source 0.5x pull, a weaker push in the same direction.
- The LT-priming cross-cue is clamped at 0 and never goes negative.
- The salience shock already has a Retreat regime that moves out-partisans -1, but its Rally regime still gives bridge-builders +0.5. The paper's consensus condition found no movement at all.

The paper does not supply a legislator-level backfire magnitude. Every transfer runs from the mass public to members of Congress and from climate to credit-union issues, so any recalibration is UNVERIFIED and remains Paul's decision.
works.question: Does out-group cueing from Democratic elites, delivered through news coverage, drive the rise of climate skepticism in the US public, especially among Republicans, and can that effect be shown to be causal rather than a by-product of confounders?
works.method: Text-as-data pipeline: Lexicoder plus a custom dictionary of party names, office titles and leaders to flag elite cues. Share of articles with Democratic cues and Republican cues. Republican cue measure is the cue share multiplied by the share of hostile Republican messages (validated against LCV scores, r=0.72). Frames via SVM (80% accuracy for cost frames, recall 0.76 and precision 0.80; 77% accuracy for uncertainty frames, recall 0.70 and precision 0.68). Time series: reduced-form VAR with lags up to four quarters (higher lag chosen when tests disagree; stability checked) and Granger causality tests, with controls for NOAA climate index, oil prices, unemployment and quarter dummies (pp. 11-13). Contemporaneous models: lagged-dependent-variable OLS with robust SEs (Eq. 1), controls for Republican cues, uncertainty and cost frames, salience (NYT plus WaPo volume), climate, oil, unemployment (Table 2). Experiment: OLS (Eq. 2) interacting five treatment dummies (Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized cues; supporting GOP cue; consensus cues) with 7-point partisanship and with controls (trust in scientists, political interest) and their interactions with treatment. Outcome is a 7-point agree/disagree item on human-caused warming, rescaled 0-1 (pp. 18-21).

findings.finding: Democratic elite cues Granger-cause aggregate climate skepticism; the reverse does not hold.
findings.numbers: Dem cues -> skepticism chi2 6.96, p=0.01 (1 lag); skepticism -> Dem cues chi2 1.01, p=0.32

findings.finding: Democratic cues Granger-cause skepticism among Republicans; the reverse does not hold.
findings.numbers: Dem cues -> GOP skepticism chi2 7.35, p=0.03 (2 lags); GOP skepticism -> Dem cues chi2 0.29, p=0.86

findings.finding: Republican cues show weak and inconsistent cue-taking: no effect on aggregate skepticism, weak effect on Republican skepticism.
findings.numbers: GOP cues -> aggregate chi2 0.00, p=0.94; GOP cues -> GOP skepticism chi2 2.94, p=0.09; skepticism -> GOP cues p=0.82 and p=0.99

findings.finding: Contemporaneous association: Democratic cues correlate with aggregate skepticism after controls, weaker in the quarterly model.
findings.numbers: Quarterly coefficient 0.02 (SE 0.01), p~0.07; 10-point rise in Dem cue share = 0.2 SD in skepticism; N=55

findings.finding: Annual aggregate model shows the same association.
findings.numbers: Coefficient 0.02 (p~0.09); 10-point rise = 0.2 SD; R2=0.89; N=28. Republican cues not significant (p~0.60)

findings.finding: Republican-specific skepticism responds to Democratic cues (H2 support) and to Republican cues.
findings.numbers: Dem cues 0.03 (p<0.01) = 0.3 SD per 10 points; GOP cues 0.04 (p~0.02) = 0.4 SD per 10 points; N=54

related.why: Noble and Turner's item covers going-public structure (Prop. 1, p. 13: going public widens the gridlock region), which the salience shock implements. Merkley and Stecula give mass-public evidence that the out-partisan retreat direction is real (polarized-cue backlash). Their consensus null is not a test of Noble's rally regime, so it does not show a rally fails to move out-partisans.

Bakker et al. (Study 1: out-party cue -0.06 on a 0-1 scale, p<.01) is the cited basis for the LT-priming cross-cue clamp. Merkley and Stecula independently find out-party cues move Republicans against the cue, on climate and in news coverage.

Box-Steffensmeier et al. study legislators taking cues from interest-group Dear Colleague letters; Merkley and Stecula study the mass public taking cues from party elites in news. Together they mark the legislator versus voter boundary for cue parameters.

Rice and Zorn's item shows corpus-based dictionaries beat standard ones (LIWC, AFINN) on specialized vocabulary, which bears on applying LSD2015 to congressional releases. Merkley and Stecula use Lexicoder with a custom party-cue dictionary validated against hand coding.

Haselmayer and Jenny pair a dictionary with crowdcoding validation (480 coders, 92% mean accuracy). Merkley and Stecula pair a dictionary with hand-coded validation of 700 articles. Whether the LSD tone layer has an equivalent validation sample was not checked (validate_stage5.R was not read).

works.title: Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting
works.summary: Tappin, Wittenberg, Hewitt, Berinsky and Rand (PNAS 2023) test whether microtargeting, meaning pretesting messages and using generalized random forests to send each covariate profile the message predicted to persuade it most, beats two simpler strategies: random messages (naive) and one pretested best message for everyone (single-best-message, SBM). In a Feb 2022 Lucid sample (5,284 U.S. adults analyzed), Study 1 on a single policy found microtargeting moved support 5.96 pp vs 3.48 SBM and 1.79 naive (precision-weighted over two modules). Almost all of that came from the Citizenship Act module (5.17 vs 2.41). The UBI module was not significant. Targeting on one covariate, such as party or ideology alone, did as well as targeting on two to four or more. In Study 2, across 36 issues, letting the targeted issue vary by person did not beat one best issue ad (12.30 vs 15.42, P=0.11), though both beat naive (6.19). The authors call the advantage highly context dependent. They say forced-exposure survey estimates probably overstate field returns, and they did not test candidate races. For Paul's systems, the closest point of contact is Terrier's Untapped potential score. It ranks whom to contact by support closeness to 0.5, chance of voting and sphere of influence. It has no message dimension and no estimate of effect size. The paper says message choice changes the effect a lot (naive was near zero in one module) and that coarse partisan targeting is enough to capture the gain. That is an extension Terrier could add cheaply, but only through its own pretest. Melange's legislator-side persuadability is barely touched: this is a mass-public survey study. Its relevance there is limited to context on low-information issues. No brain rule is in conflict.
works.question: Does political microtargeting (message pretesting combined with machine learning, so each person sees the message predicted to persuade them most) produce a persuasive advantage over a naive random-message strategy and a single-best-message strategy? Does targeting by more covariates, or targeting issues rather than messages on one issue, add returns?
works.method: Calibration: for each covariate profile (255 profiles from 8 covariates in Study 1; 511 profiles from 9 covariates in Study 2), generalized random forests (grf R package) trained on 75 percent of data estimate message-level heterogeneity. The message predicted best for each subgroup is evaluated on the 25 percent test set by restricting the treatment group to people assigned their predicted-best message and comparing to control. Monte Carlo cross-validation: 250 random splits; median per profile; top profile in each stratum (1, 2-3, or 4+ covariates) refit on full data. Single-best-message = message with largest OLS ATE in training data. Experimental phase: OLS with condition dummies vs control, robust (HC2) SEs. Study 2: separate OLS per strategy, then difference-in-differences interaction models.

findings.finding: Study 1, U.S. Citizenship Act: microtargeting produced over twice the persuasive impact of single-best-message, and far more than naive messaging.
Study 1, UBI: microtargeting point estimates favor it over both alternatives but are not statistically significant.
Study 1 precision-weighted across both modules: microtargeting advantage is about 70 percent larger than SBM and over 200 percent larger than naive.

No evidence that targeting by more covariates increases persuasive returns; the advantage was qualitatively largest with one covariate, though differences were slight. Coarse targeting by party or ideology alone produced an advantage.
findings.numbers: Fig 2 profile values not mapped in text; differences described as relatively slight

findings.finding: Study 2, multi-issue: microtargeting is directionally but not significantly below single-best-message, and clearly above naive messaging.
findings.location: p.6, Study 2 Experimental Phase; Fig 3, p.6

findings.finding: Study 2 conclusion: targeting different issues to different people was not more impactful than distributing one pretested ad on one issue to everyone, though pretested targeting clearly beat naive.

related.why: Simchon et al test matching ad style to reader openness and whether LLMs can mass-produce matched ads, which fits the generative-AI extension. Tappin supplies the pretest-and-target baseline. The one-covariate finding is Tappin's own result, not Simchon's.

Broockman and Kalla argue that returns to moderation depend on where voters are, which echoes Tappin's context-dependent results. Their working paper covers candidate races, which Tappin did not test.

Palm and Tims review how personality traits moderate persuasion strategies. Tappin's Study 1 moral-foundation profiles did not beat one-covariate targeting, which is a check on rich psychological tailoring.

works.title: Crypto-Oligarchy: The Cryptocurrency Lobby in American Politics
works.summary:
Chohan's discussion paper is an essay, not an empirical study. It describes Fairshake, the crypto super PAC network that also includes Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, and argues that the industry has moved from crypto-anarchism through statism to an 'oligarchic' stage, using a Marxian stage model. Its numbers come from the press or from Fairshake itself: $203M raised for the 2024 cycle (p. 7), 253 supported candidates with no win rate and no counterfactual (p. 8), $78M already raised toward 2026 (p. 9), and an unsourced count of 100,000 crypto millionaires (p. 14). It names targeted races: Moreno over Brown in Ohio, against Tester in Montana, against Porter in a primary and against Bowman. It says these show 'decisive' influence (pp. 9-10) but estimates nothing, and it notes that many of the ads never mentioned crypto (p. 8).

For Paul's systems the paper adds no measurement or method. Its value is descriptive, and it points the same way in three places.

1. **Crypto money flows mostly through super PACs.** It is corporate-treasury money aimed at elections and often spent against candidates, not PAC contributions to candidate committees. That fits Mentat keeping a separate Super PAC channel and a support/oppose field. It also shows that Melange's flip model cannot see this money at all, because its industry money term counts only direct bank and finserv PAC receipts.
2. **The series breaks in 2024.** A new entrant spent at record scale in its first big cycle, which supports the registry decision to decline a crypto forecast for now.
3. **Primary-contest plays exist in practice.** Industry money has been used to contest primaries, the same kind of play the electoral-plays module models.

None of the paper's claims about effects on outcomes can be used as evidence. That applies especially to the competitiveness multiplier, where reciprocity is still not validated.
