works.title: The strategic advantages of micro-targeted campaigning: A proof of principle Bayesian Agent-Based Model
works.summary:
Madsen and Pilditch build a small agent-based model as a proof of concept. Two candidates compete over 50 ticks for 10,000 simulated voters who are not connected to each other. Each contacted voter replaces its belief with a Bayesian source-credibility posterior. Credibility is split into expertise and trustworthiness, and the conditional probabilities come from Madsen (2016) with no free parameters. The micro-targeted campaign contacts only voters whose mean credibility score for it is above 0.5, 20 per tick. The stochastic campaign contacts voters at random, with reach set to 1 to 10 times the targeted campaign's.

Results:
- At equal reach, targeting wins.
- When mean credibility is 0.5, random contact is wasted, because contacts land on favourable and unfavourable voters in equal numbers.
- A random campaign with about twice the reach cancels the targeting advantage.
- Above a 2x reach ratio, and with credibility above 0.5, the random campaign wins.

All results come from one figure. The paper reports no replications, no intervals and no sensitivity analysis, and it does not model turnout, multiple issues, or voter-to-voter networks.

For Paul's systems this is weak evidence about mechanism, not a calibration source. It agrees with two design choices: contacts go only to receptive targets, and money is never spent trying to convert opponents. Both match the paper's finding that blind contact with low-credibility audiences is inefficient or harmful. It also says the advantage of targeting depends on reach, which no part of the system models. The closest analogue is Terrier's untapped-potential score for door canvassing. That score gives persuasion weight to undecided likely voters but carries no credibility or receptivity term for the messenger. That missing term is the variable that decides the paper's result. The paper does not touch the cosponsorship network, LDA, reciprocity, or the rank pillars. It gives no reason to change a constant. Every number it reports is a simulation output, not an estimate.
works.question: Does a micro-targeted campaign (MTC), which contacts only voters with a favourable view of the candidate's credibility, persuade the electorate more efficiently than a stochastic campaign that contacts voters at random? Can an agent-based model with a Bayesian source-credibility belief-updating rule simulate persuasion campaign strategies? The paper frames itself as an exploratory proof of concept.
works.method: Agent-based model (ABM) with two agent types, voters and persuaders. Persuaders are either MTC or stochastic (non-MTC). Voters are randomly distributed, with no spatial role, and have no links to each other. Persuaders make direct contacts. The non-MTC candidate contacts voters at random and states p(candidate) = 1. The MTC candidate contacts only voters whose signal factor (mean of T and E) exceeds 0.5, sampling randomly among eligible voters up to its reach, and states p(candidate) = 0. Each contacted voter replaces its belief with the posterior P(candidate|rep). A voter is contacted at most once per tick. At the end, each voter votes for the candidate it favours (p > 0.5). Design: 2 x 2 manipulation of mean credibility (0.5 or 0.6) crossed with non-MTC reach ratio 1 to 10. Outcome is the share of voters supporting the non-MTC candidate. Results are presented as a single figure (Fig. 2). No statistical tests, confidence intervals or sensitivity analysis are reported.

findings.finding: Under the Bayesian source-credibility rule, an MTC with the same reach consistently beats a stochastic campaign.
findings.numbers: MTC reach fixed at 20 per tick; non-MTC reach ratio 1 to 10 (ratio 1 = equal reach). Exact vote shares are only in Fig. 2 and are not given in the text.

findings.finding: With mean credibility 0.5, a stochastic (non-MTC) campaign is inefficient. Opinions are equally split, so blind contacts reach supporters and opponents in equal numbers. Blind campaigns only work when the candidate's average perceived credibility is above 0.5. Below that, they can be ineffective or harmful.
findings.numbers: Mean credibility 0.5 versus 0.6 (SD 0.25).

findings.finding: A non-MTC campaign with roughly double the reach cancels out the MTC advantage.
findings.numbers: Break-even at non-MTC reach about 2x the MTC reach (MTC reach = 20).

findings.finding: If the non-MTC reach ratio exceeds 2 and the non-MTC candidate's perceived credibility is above 0.5, the stochastic campaign beats the strategic one.
findings.numbers: Reach ratio > 2; credibility mean > 0.5.

findings.finding: Discussion restates that the MTC advantage is not general: a positively perceived stochastic candidate with greater reach can beat a strategic one.
findings.numbers: Non-MTC needs double reach to cancel the advantage.

findings.finding: The authors predict, without testing, that MTC efficiency rises with available voter data and with electorate complexity (belief systems, individual differences, voter-to-voter interaction). MTC costs are also predicted to rise with complexity.
findings.numbers: None reported; this is a prediction only.

related.why: Tappin measures persuasive returns to microtargeting with experiments; Madsen and Pilditch only simulate them. Tappin is the empirical check on this paper's claim that targeting has an advantage.
Simchon also studies the persuasive effects of political microtargeting, with generative-AI messages. It offers the empirical evidence this paper does not have.
Both make contact conditional on the target's receptivity. Chen does it as contingency-aware seeding, which the system implements as SGATE; this paper does it as credibility-gated contact.
A two-candidate competitive voter-dynamics model on networks. It adds the voter-to-voter interaction this paper leaves out and says targeting would benefit from.

works.title: CampaignView, a database of policy platforms and biographical narratives for congressional candidates
works.summary: Porter, Case and Treul (Scientific Data 2025) release CampaignView, a data descriptor rather than a hypothesis test: campaign-website text for U.S. House major-party primary candidates in 2018, 2020 and 2022. Of 6,016 ballot-eligible candidates, 5,228 (86.9%) are in the corpus, giving 43,465 platform points and 5,114 biographies. Text was scraped about one week before each primary, with Wayback Machine backfill (7.8% of candidates). Every platform point is hand-coded into one of 14 policy topics. On a 20% relabel sample (8,584 points) agreement is 80% and Cohen kappa is 0.84. Rows carry FEC and BioGuide IDs, and candidate names were linked across cycles by embedding-based record linkage. Missingness is not random: across the 6,016 candidates, 11.9% have no website and 25.1% have no platform, and incumbents, unopposed candidates and better-funded candidates are much less likely to be missing (Table 5 logit, associations only). In descriptive platform shares, Democrats emphasize environment, healthcare and social welfare, while Republicans emphasize immigration and government operations. For Paul's systems the paper has no network, lobbying or allocation content. It matters in two places. First, the electoral-plays contest-primary route scores an Opponent's primary vulnerability against the same-party average CU score, not against any real challenger. CampaignView gives candidate-level challenger platforms that could replace that proxy for House seats in 2018-2022. Second, its hand-coded topic labels with reported reliability are a template for the open question of how precise the press-release regex topic tagger is. Coverage limits: House only, three cycles, website text only. The topic codes do not map to credit-union categories.
works.question: No hypothesis is tested. The paper asks how to supply systematic, real-time text of congressional candidate campaign websites (platforms and biographies) for 2018 to 2022 House primaries, so that questions on polarization, agenda-setting and representation can be studied (Abstract p.1; Background p.2).
works.method: Descriptive data construction. Name standardization by probabilistic record linkage on pretrained word embeddings, blocked on party and state; matches under 50% probability hand-checked (p.8-9). Every platform point hand-labeled into one of 14 Major Policy Topic codes by trained annotators with a codebook (p.3). Topic term lists from keyness analysis (Table 2, p.7). Missingness described by logistic regression of website, biography and platform absence on covariates (Table 5, p.9). Relabeling check on a 20% random sample (8,584 points) by other coders (p.10).

findings.finding: Corpus covers 5,228 candidates, 86.9% of 6,016 eligible House primary candidates, 2018-2022; 43,465 platform points and 5,114 biographies.
Campaign website identified for 5,300 candidates (88.1%); 85.0% of those had a platform and 96.5% a biography.
Missingness: no biography for 14.99%, no platform for 25.08%, no website at all for 11.9% of the 6,016 candidates.
Archived Wayback data supplies 7.8% of candidates; 239 in 2018, 101 in 2020, 67 in 2022. 1,111 candidates (18.5%) had no primary-season data.
Unopposed primary is negatively associated with missing website, biography and platform (-0.342, -0.349, -0.320; all significant at 95%).

Current incumbent MC has the largest negative association with missing website (-2.967), biography (-2.000) and platform (-0.314). Logged fundraising is negative for all three (-0.222, -0.194, -0.136).

related.why: Vault summary confirms Bonica's CFscores are donor-based candidate ideal points. The pairing with CampaignView platform text is the analyst's suggestion; the paper does not cite Bonica.
Vault title and summary confirm a study of when moving to the middle wins votes. CampaignView is a candidate-level source of primary positions, as the analyst says; the paper does not cite Broockman.

Vault file confirms it is about LLMs for political texts (Political Science Research and Methods, 2025). The analyst's use as a scalable check on CampaignView's hand codes is a suggestion, not a claim in either paper.

works.title: Simulated redistricting plans for the analysis and evaluation of redistricting in the United States
works.summary: McCartan, Kenny, Simko, Garcia, Wang, Wu, Kuriwaki and Imai (Scientific Data 9:689, 2022) is a data descriptor for the 50stateSimulations dataset. For each state's congressional map it gives 5,000 simulated 2020-cycle plans, drawn with the Sequential Monte Carlo sampler in the redist R package. The hard constraints are contiguity, at most 0.5 percent population deviation, and county splits capped at districts minus one. Soft constraints cover compactness and matching the enacted plan's count of minority-opportunity districts. Precinct-level VEST election returns are crosswalked onto 2020 Census blocks. The enacted plan is read as a possible gerrymander when it is an outlier against this ensemble. In the Georgia example (14 districts, 20,000 plans sampled and thinned to 5,000), the enacted 12th and 14th districts have 2020 presidential Democratic two-party shares above the simulated range, which suggests packing. The paper tests no substantive hypothesis. It warns that its partisan metrics depend on which statewide elections exist in each state and cannot be compared across states. Two authors disclose paid expert-witness work. For Paul's systems the bearing is narrow. Nothing here covers lobbying, PAC money, networks or persuasion. The work touches the system only where district geography enters. (1) The competitiveness multiplier c uses a single Cook PVI point per seat. It flags the 10 mid-decade-redistricted states but never adjusts them. The dataset could supply a map-dependence baseline, but only for 2020-cycle maps, not the 2025-26 redraws. (2) The census district metrics mix 119th-Congress ACS with 116th-Congress CBP boundaries. The paper's precinct-to-block crosswalk is a reusable template for re-aggregation. It does not measure the error that this mismatch causes. Both bearings are weak. Paul has no annotations on this work. The analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: How can analysts run a complete, reproducible redistricting simulation analysis for the congressional districts of all 50 states, and what do simulated 2020-cycle plans show about enacted maps? The paper is a data descriptor: it documents the dataset, code and validation rather than testing a substantive hypothesis (p.1-2).
works.method: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm from the redist R package (McCartan and Imai 2021). Hard constraints: contiguity; population deviation at most 0.5 percent (about 3,826 people in Georgia); county or municipality splits capped at districts minus one. Soft constraints: default compactness, untuned in most states; minority opportunity districts matched to the enacted plan (Georgia: soft 52 percent BVAP target). Most states combine two samples of 2,500 (p.3-4). Diagnostics: resampling weights, variation of information, bottleneck checks, Gelman-Rubin R about 1.05 or less (p.7).
findings: Georgia 2020 enacted plan: two of its 14 ordered districts (12th and 14th) have 2020 presidential Democratic two-party vote shares above the range of the 5,000 simulated plans; the authors suggest packing may exceed what traditional criteria require (p.8, Fig. 2).
Remaining Georgia enacted districts fall within the simulated range on 2020 presidential Democratic share (p.8, Fig. 2).
Georgia: 20,000 plans sampled, then 5,000 kept by random sampling after convergence diagnostics passed (p.3, p.4).
Population deviation limit of 0.5 percent corresponds to about 3,826 people in Georgia; precinct-level units are used rather than blocks (p.3).
Compactness is not tuned to the enacted map in most states; Florida and North Carolina final simulations are less compact than the enacted maps, while Illinois simulations are more compact (p.6-7).

Georgia sampler diagnostics: Gelman-Rubin R of about 1.05 or less is the convergence threshold for all summary statistics; no numeric variation-of-information value for Georgia is reported in the text (p.7-8).

related.why: Both use ensembles of algorithmically sampled districting plans as the neutral baseline for judging maps and criteria.
Best asks whether commissions avoid partisan gerrymanders. McCartan supplies the outlier-versus-ensemble benchmark such an evaluation needs.
DeLuca validates BISG race estimation for redistricting. McCartan's VRA constraint relies on district minority VAP shares, the measurement DeLuca's method addresses.
The SMC sampler and its convergence diagnostics (Gelman-Rubin R of about 1.05 or less, resampling weights) extend the basic Monte Carlo sampling that Harrison introduces.

works.title: Small Campaign Donors
works.summary: Bouton, Cage, Dewitte and Pons (NBER WP 30050, revised June 2026) build a contribution-level panel of about 340 million FEC individual contributions (2005-2020) by parsing ActBlue and WinRed earmark memos, which makes sub-200-dollar donors visible. Their main finding is that small donors are a passive force. They tripled to 21.8 million by 2020 but supplied only 12.8 percent of 2020 money. They back the same kinds of candidates as large donors, send about 88 percent of their money out of district, and do not concentrate on close races (close-seat coefficient +0.11 pp, not significant, versus +0.18 pp for large donors; Democratic congressional candidates 2012-2020). Their giving spikes on salient events, while large donors spike at quarterly deadlines. TV ads raise small-dollar giving by 6.3 percent of the mean per 1,000 ads, and Meta ads do so only in primaries. For Paul's systems the substantive results are background. The data appendix matters more for Mentat. First, it documents that an earmarked gift from a donor above the 200-dollar aggregate appears in both the conduit report and the recipient committee report. The authors pair and drop 87 percent of these duplicates, whereas Mentat counts both legs under ruling R8; this is flagged, not recommended. Second, the donor-grouping rules always require a street address and reject employer and occupation as grouping keys. Mentat's identity ladder auto-accepts on exact name plus ZIP alone. Third, conduit coverage changes over time (76.4 percent of contributions 2006-2020, 91.1 percent in 2020, WinRed only from 2019), so cross-cycle partisan comparisons of employee giving carry a visibility artifact. The paper says nothing about whether dollars buy access or alignment.
works.question: Are small campaign donors (giving at most 200 dollars to any committee per two-year cycle) a new force that could transform U.S. elections, in terms of their number, sociodemographic profile, candidate and race targeting, and responsiveness to events and ads?
works.method: Section 2: descriptive counts with imputed unobserved unitemized totals. Section 3: descriptive comparison of gender, ethnicity, occupation, wage, home value and geography. Section 4: OLS linear probability model of the share of a donor's contributions going to a candidate (equation 1), with election year, state, House/Senate and donor fixed effects, two-way clustered at seat and donor. Section 4.5: Herfindahl-Hirschman index by donor decile. Section 5.1: weekly timing and abnormal-week flags. Section 5.2: TV ads via border-county pairs in different DMAs (Spenkuch and Toniatti 2018 design), OLS with county-pair-by-year and county-by-office fixed effects, clustered at DMA. Section 5.3: social media ads event study with the heterogeneity-robust de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2024) estimator, week-state fixed effects, clustered at candidate-week.
findings: Small donors rose from 5.0 million (2006 cycle) to 21.8 million (2020); large donors rose from 2.3 million to 7.0 million (Section 2.2, p. 9).

Small donor contributions were 12.8 percent of all contributions in the 2020 cycle and 14.9 percent for Democratic congressional candidates; small contributions grew from 362 million to 1.664 billion dollars 2006-2020 versus large from 2.084 to 11.307 billion (Section 2.2, p. 10).
Unitemized contribution totals overstate small donor contributions by a factor of 1.8 to 3.1 (Section 2.2, p. 8).

Among Democratic congressional donors 2012-2020, 23.1 percent of small donors are non-white, about 13 percent more than large donors, but 42.1 percent less than the voting-age population; small donors are 56.9 percent female versus 47.2 percent for large donors (Section 3, p. 12, Table 2).

Median 2020 home value is 289,900 dollars for small donors, 419,910 for large donors and 176,838 for the population; 44.5 percent of small donors have high-SOC occupations versus 54.1 percent for large donors (Table 2, p. 13).

About 88 percent of small-donor contributions go to out-of-district candidates; same-district matching raises small donor shares by 16.8 percentage points versus 20.4 for large donors (Section 4.1-4.3, p. 17-18).

related.why: Bouton et al. use Bonica's CFscores for candidate ideology terciles and describe them as built from contribution records. The paper cites Bonica 2014 (AJPS); the vault note dates the work 2013 (SSRN draft), so the year label differs. Their close-race result is Democratic-only, so it bears on Bonica's donor-steering account only for Democratic individual donors 2012-2020.

Bouton et al. cite Kalla and Broockman (2016), a randomized field experiment titled Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials, in their introduction on elite responsiveness. Bouton et al. study where donor money goes, not whether it buys access.

Bouton et al. describe small donors as responding to candidate fundraising requests and external events. Cagala et al. (2021, arXiv, Optimal Targeting in Fundraising) study the supply side of solicitation. Bouton et al. do not cite this work, so the link is a vault-level complement.

works.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
works.summary: Ansolabehere, de Figueiredo and Snyder (NBER WP 9409, 2002) restate the Tullock puzzle. In 2000 about 3 billion dollars went to campaigns, against 2 trillion of federal spending. They answer that campaign money is mostly individual consumption and participation, not policy purchase. Individuals gave about 2.4 of the 3 billion dollars. Only 4 percent of PAC gifts are near the limit. In nearly 40 roll-call studies, PAC effects are null or wrongly signed three times in four. In their own House panel (1978-1994, N = 3400), 60000 dollars of corporate PAC money moves a 0-100 Chamber score by at most 2 points, while party moves it by more than 30. District fixed effects nearly remove the money effect, member fixed effects remove it entirely, and IV reverses the corporate sign. Spending tracks income: the gubernatorial income elasticity is about 1.1, the stakes (government spending) have no effect, and closeness raises spending. Executives give about 0.05 percent of income, close to the national rate. For Paul's systems the paper is load-bearing. The Melange money engine already cites Ansolabehere to justify cutting MAXSHIFT from 40 to 18 and weighting money below peers. The paper supports that cut on votes. It does not support the access half of the code comment, and it gives no evidence that dollars buy more in competitive seats: closeness raises the supply of money, mostly small individual gifts. On the Mentat side, the consumption account fits the sector growth study's null for industry growth and suggests that donor or national income, not industry revenue, scales giving.
works.question: Why is there so little money in U.S. politics given the large value of policies at stake (Tullock 1972 puzzle), and why do organized interests give at all? The authors argue that campaign giving is mainly consumption and participation by individuals, not investment in legislation.
works.method: Descriptive accounting of contributions by source; tabulation of prior roll-call studies by significance and sign; OLS and two-stage IV regressions of the CCUS score on corporate and labor PAC money with year effects and either party plus district preference, district fixed effects, or member fixed effects; OLS state fixed-effects panel of log per-capita gubernatorial spending; cross-section regressions of House race spending on district income and margin with year, party and incumbency controls; time-series ratios of spending to GDP and national income.
findings: Individuals gave nearly 2.4 billion of about 3 billion dollars in 1999-2000; about 21 million people (about 10 percent of adults) gave, averaging about 115 dollars (p.7).
Only 4 percent of PAC contributions to House and Senate candidates are at or near the 10000 dollar limit; the average PAC gift is 1700 dollars and the modal contribution is zero (p.8).

In 2000 PACs spent 579.4 million dollars in total; 280.8 million went to or for candidates and about 300 million to overhead and other activity that could have been paid by the sponsor's treasury (p.9).
In a survey of nearly 40 roll-call studies, PAC contributions had no significant effect or the wrong sign in three of four instances (Table 1, p.15).

CCUS model, House 1978-1994, N = 3400: an extra 60000 dollars of corporate PAC money (about one SD) moves the 0-100 score by at most 2 points, while a change of party moves it more than 30 points (pp.18-19).
District fixed effects nearly eliminate the contribution effects, and member fixed effects eliminate them entirely; coefficients are tiny and insignificant in OLS and IV (Table 2, p.19).

related.why: Randomized field experiment (Kalla and Broockman) on donor access to congressional officials. It supplies the access half of the engine's citation, which this paper only hypothesizes. Item exists.

Lobbying ROI analysis under the 2004 American Jobs Creation Act. Its text reports positive, significant lobbying returns, set against this paper's small-return account. The link is a framing contrast, not a direct test. Item exists.
Reports minimal overlap between organizations that lobby and those that make PAC expenditures. It is a check on this paper's claim that big givers also lobby heavily. Item exists.
Studies small individual donors, the consumer contributor this paper puts at the center of campaign finance. Item exists.
Shows ideologically sorted donors, consistent with giving as ideological participation. Item exists.
Fouirnaies and Hall on electoral incentives in U.S. state legislatures. Bears on the competitiveness lever, but for state, not federal, legislators. Item exists.
Links donation timing to lobbying, which complicates a pure consumption reading for organized interests. Item exists.
A co-author's later review of lobbying empirics. The claim that lobbying spending dwarfs PAC giving was not found in its text, so only the agenda link stands. Item exists.
Paul's sector growth source note. The paper's null for stakes and its income elasticity bear on the growth-giving hypothesis. Item exists.

works.title: Partisan Impacts on the Economy: Evidence from Prediction Markets and Close Elections
works.summary: Snowberg, Wolfers and Zitzewitz (IZA DP 1996, 2006; later QJE 2007) estimate how U.S. presidential outcomes move asset prices. Their key move is identification: on election nights 2004 and 2000, shocks to the market probability of a Bush win (a faulty afternoon exit poll that cut his odds from about 55 to 30 percent and then reversed; the Florida calls in 2000) are treated as exogenous, and asset changes are divided by probability changes (Wald ratios). In 2004 a Bush win raised S&P futures about 1.5-2 percent (0.016 at 10-minute differences, n=104), 10-year yields 11-12 basis points and December 2004 oil about 1.07 dollars. Over 1880-2004 a market-based partisan surprise (Republican indicator minus pre-election probability) implies 2-3 percent higher equities under a Republican president. The methodological lesson matters most for Paul: a daily campaign-period regression of prices on win probabilities gave equity coefficients about ten times the election-night estimate and flipped the oil sign, because the economy moves the odds (reverse causation) and common news moves both. OLS is only an upper bound if political and economic shocks correlate non-negatively. For Mentat this bears on the sector growth study: SEATS-W regresses weekly Democratic giving share on prior-week changes in 538 expected seats (2022 House, -3.47 pp per seat, one election, EXPLORATORY), and SHIFT uses expected-minus-current control. Lagging the forecast fixes ordering but not common shocks, so SEATS-W is a correlation, not a donor response. The paper also suggests a sharper design: event windows around discrete forecast jumps and a surprise-coded shock. It says nothing about networks, lobbying or ranks.
works.question: Do U.S. presidential election outcomes (a Republican versus Democratic winner, and Bush versus Kerry or Gore) causally move equity prices, bond yields, oil prices and the dollar?
works.method: OLS of change in log financial variable on change in re-election probability, 10- and 30-minute first differences, inverse-period weights, White SEs (Scholes-Williams and 60-minute checks similar). Newey-West SEs for daily, 5-day and 20-day campaign regressions. Two-equation structural system with OLS bound. Wald ratio for yields using TIP and IEF funds. Historical event study of returns on a GOP indicator and partisan shock, plus an incumbent-party term.
findings: 2004 election night (Table 1, p.7): Bush-versus-Kerry effect on log S&P 500 futures is 0.016 (SE 0.004, n=104) at 10-minute differences and 0.020 (SE 0.005, n=35) at 30-minute differences; text says equity prices 1.5 to 2 percent higher under Bush.

Table 1, p.7: Dow 0.014 and Nasdaq 100 0.019 at 10 minutes (both significant at 1 percent); Nasdaq 0.024 at 30 minutes. Dollar 0.004 (not significant) at 10 minutes and 0.005 (5 percent) at 30 minutes.
Table 1, p.7: December 2004 crude oil futures rise by 1.07 dollars (SE 0.35, 1 percent) at 10 minutes and 1.63 (SE 0.59) at 30 minutes; December 2006 contract is negative and insignificant.
Table 1, p.7-8: 2-year note 0.095 (10 percent) and 10-year note 0.108 (5 percent) at 10 minutes; text says 10-year yields 11-12 basis points and 2-year yields 10 basis points higher under Bush.

TIP and IEF Wald estimates, p.8-9: real yields about 16 basis points higher under Bush from the exit-poll experiment and 11 from the second; nominal about 16 and 15, so the authors conclude nominal moves mostly reflect expected real rates, consistent with expansionary fiscal policy.

Exit-poll episode, p.5-6: Bush win probability fell from about 55 to 30 percent with stocks down about one percent, then rebounded to 95 percent as the exit poll was found faulty and stocks rebounded.

related.why: Furnas et al. estimate revenue effects for party-tied lobbying firms after House-control flips, a control-shock design close to the SEATS and SHIFT question; the outcome is firm revenue, not donations.
Imai and Kim show that two-way fixed-effects estimates rely on linearity for a causal reading, which bounds what the SHIFT and SEATS-W panel regressions can claim.
